title: Proposition 5: Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.

context.text: Placed on the ballot by the Legislature as SCA 1 (Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024). Final legislative votes: Senate 32 ayes, 8 noes; Assembly 59 ayes, 17 noes.

question.text: CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT. Under current law, voters decide at the same election whether (1) to recall a state officer, and (2) who will replace that officer if recalled. Under this measure: if the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor for the remainder of the term or until a successor is elected; for all other recalled officers, the office will remain vacant until filled by a subsequent special election or appointment as specified in existing law; and a recalled officer may be a candidate in a special election to fill the office.

summary.text: Removes the second question (who should replace the official) from state-level recall elections. If a recall succeeds, the office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules: typically a special election for Senate or Assembly seats and gubernatorial appointment for other offices. If the Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor; if the recall occurs early enough in the term, voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election, otherwise the Lieutenant Governor serves the rest of the term. Fiscal impact per the Legislative Analyst: net effect unknown; possible state and local savings or costs of millions of dollars per recall election, depending on the office recalled and how often recalls occur.

measure.yesMeans: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
measure.noMeans: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.

argumentsFor.text: Official argument in favor, signed by Lorrel Plimier (League of Women Voters of California), Darius L. Kemp (California Common Cause) and Dan Schnur (former Chair, Fair Political Practices Commission): "Proposition 5 makes a single, commonsense change: it removes the second question from the recall ballot."
Same argument, citing the 2021 gubernatorial recall: "had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with support from only about 28% of all recall voters."

argumentsAgainst.text: Official argument against, signed by Senate Minority Leader Brian W. Jones and Assemblymember Joe Patterson: "Proposition 5 keeps the first part but eliminates your ability to vote for a replacement."
Same argument: "In many cases, politicians themselves—not voters—would choose who fills the vacancy" and in other cases "the seat would sit vacant until another costly election."

currentLaw.text: In a recall election of a state official, voters are asked two questions: whether to remove the official and who should replace them; the candidate with the most votes on the second question takes office. Since 1913, 11 state recall efforts have qualified for the ballot (nine legislators and two Governors); six led to removal (five legislators and one Governor). Other vacancies are filled by special election (Assembly and Senate) or gubernatorial appointment (most other offices); the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor when that office is vacant.

fiscalImpact.text: Per the Legislative Analyst: the net fiscal effect is unknown because it depends on future recalls. Costs could rise if a standalone special election were needed to fill a vacancy (potentially "millions of dollars per election"); savings could result from removing replacement candidates from recall ballots (also potentially millions per election). The range is less than 0.1 percent of the General Fund budget.

campaignFinance.text: Per the Secretary of State's ballot-measure contribution totals, no committees primarily formed to support or oppose Proposition 5 had been identified as of October 6, 2026.
